canonical_topic: Estimation risk in solar project sizing
definition: Because a solar installation's economics hinge on correctly forecasting how much power it will produce, both under- and over-estimating output create distinct failure modes for a project.
core_idea: Solar output forecasts sit on a knife's edge: too conservative an estimate makes a viable project look uneconomical and it gets shelved for other technologies, while too optimistic an estimate leads to a shortfall that fails to meet the installation's economic targets.
key_points: Overly conservative production estimates can cause solar to be passed over in favor of other generation technologies even when it would have been viable.
Overly optimistic production estimates create a power shortfall relative to the economic goals set for the installation.

Historical, government-collected regional/national solar radiation averages are the standard tool used to make these estimates, because insolation varies with weather, sun position, and day length throughout the year.
relationships: Ties to government renewable-incentive programs mentioned in the chapter purpose, since incentives shape whether marginal projects proceed.
trading_implications: Investment/financing decisions for solar projects are directly sensitive to the quality of the underlying irradiance forecast — this is the core diligence item for evaluating a proposed installation.
caveats: Treating solar output forecasting as a minor engineering detail rather than the critical determinant of whether a project is even worth building.
